title: TypeScript with React
summary: **TypeScript with React** adds static types to components, props, state, refs, events, and hooks — catching whole classes of bugs at compile time and turning your editor into a live contract for how each component must be used.

subtopics.title: Typing props
subtopics.explanation: Props are the public API of a component, so you describe their exact shape with an interface or type and annotate the parameter directly: function Button(props: ButtonProps). The compiler then verifies every <Button /> call site — flagging missing required props, misspellings, and wrong types before the code runs. Prefer this over React.FC, which adds an implicit children prop and complicates generics.
subtopics.example: interface ButtonProps { label: string; onClick: () => void; disabled?: boolean; }\nfunction Button({ label, onClick, disabled = false }: ButtonProps) { /* ... */ }

subtopics.title: ReactNode children
subtopics.explanation: When a component wraps arbitrary content, type its children as React.ReactNode — the broadest renderable type, covering JSX, strings, numbers, arrays, fragments, and null. Avoid the narrower JSX.Element (rejects strings/arrays) or React.ReactElement. This is the idiomatic way to type layout, card, and provider components.
subtopics.example:
interface CardProps { children: React.ReactNode; }\nfunction Card({ children }: CardProps) { return
{children}
; }

subtopics.title: Typing hooks
subtopics.explanation: Hooks are generic functions whose type argument tells the compiler what value they hold. useState infers from the initial value but needs an explicit generic when the eventual type is broader — useState(null) infers null and useState([]) infers never[]. useRef<HTMLInputElement>(null) types a DOM ref whose .current is T | null and must be guarded.
subtopics.example: const [user, setUser] = useState<User | null>(null);\nconst [tags, setTags] = useState<string[]>([]);\nconst inputRef = useRef<HTMLInputElement>(null);

subtopics.title: Event types
subtopics.explanation: DOM handlers receive React's synthetic event types parameterized by the element, so fields like e.target.value are correctly typed. Use React.ChangeEvent<HTMLInputElement> for inputs, React.MouseEvent for clicks, and React.FormEvent for form submits. Getting the element generic right is what makes e.target.value a string instead of any.
subtopics.example: const onChange = (e: React.ChangeEvent<HTMLInputElement>) => setText(e.target.value);\nconst onSubmit = (e: React.FormEvent) => { e.preventDefault(); };

subtopics.title: Generic components
subtopics.explanation: A generic component works for any item type while keeping callbacks fully typed. You declare a type parameter <T,> and TypeScript infers T from the props at each call site, so a renderItem callback receives a precisely-typed item. This is how reusable List, Table, and Select components stay type-safe without falling back to any.
subtopics.example:
function List({ items, renderItem }: { items: T[]; renderItem: (item: T) => React.ReactNode }) {\n return
    {items.map((it, i) =>
  • {renderItem(it)}
    • )}
;\n}

subtopics.title: Discriminated unions
subtopics.explanation: A discriminated (tagged) union models mutually exclusive prop combinations using a shared literal field. It expresses 'these props are required together' in a way a flat interface with optional fields cannot — making invalid states unrepresentable rather than caught at runtime. TypeScript narrows the union by the discriminant inside the component and at the call site.
subtopics.example: type BannerProps =\n  | { variant: 'info'; message: string }\n  | { variant: 'action'; message: string; onConfirm: () => void };

subtopics.title: Default props and optional fields
subtopics.explanation: Mark optional props with ? and supply defaults in the destructure rather than scattering undefined checks through the body. The modern pattern (with function components) is parameter defaults — React.defaultProps is legacy and discouraged for function components. This keeps the prop both optional at the call site and concrete inside.
subtopics.example: interface Props { label: string; size?: 'sm' | 'lg'; }\nfunction Tag({ label, size = 'sm' }: Props) { return {label}; }

subtopics.title: any vs unknown and type assertions
subtopics.explanation: any disables type checking for a value and silently spreads through your code, defeating the point of TypeScript. Prefer unknown for untrusted input, which forces a narrowing check before use, and validate external data (fetch responses) with a schema before trusting its type. A type assertion (as User) lies to the compiler and gives no runtime guarantee — never assert past untrusted input.
subtopics.example: const data: unknown = await res.json();\nif (isUser(data)) { /* data is User here */ }  // narrow, don't assert

foundations.overview: TypeScript layers a static type system on top of JavaScript. In React, that means you describe the exact shape of a component's props, the type of every piece of state, the kind of element a ref points at, and the events your handlers receive. The compiler then verifies — before the code ever runs — that every component is used correctly.
foundations.formalDefinition: Typing React is the practice of annotating component inputs and internal values with TypeScript types: props are described with an `interface` or `type`, components are typed as functions returning `JSX.Element` (or via `React.FC`), state and refs receive explicit generic type arguments (`useState<T>`, `useRef<T>`), and DOM events use React's synthetic event types such as `React.ChangeEvent<HTMLInputElement>`.
foundations.whyItMatters: JavaScript has no way to express 'this component requires a string title and an optional onClose callback', so misspelled props, missing required props, and wrong event fields only surface at runtime. TypeScript encodes those contracts. On any team larger than one, types are documentation that cannot go stale: autocomplete shows exactly which props a component takes, and refactors (renaming a prop, changing a callback signature) light up every call site that needs updating. This is why most production React codebases are written in TypeScript.
foundations.mentalModel: Think of each component as a function with a typed signature. The props interface is the parameter list; the compiler refuses to 'call' the component (render the JSX) unless you supply arguments of the right shape. Hooks are generic functions whose type argument tells the compiler what the box holds.
foundations.browserPerspective: Types are a build-time-only concern. TypeScript is compiled (transpiled) to plain JavaScript and every annotation is erased — the browser never sees a single type. Nothing about runtime behavior changes; the value is entirely in the feedback you get before shipping.
foundations.realWorldUsage: Typed prop interfaces for shared UI components, typed form state and change handlers, generic list/table/select components that work for any item type, typed custom hooks that return a tuple or object, and discriminated unions to model components that have mutually exclusive prop combinations.
foundations.businessImpact: Catching a wrong-prop or undefined-field bug at compile time costs seconds; catching it as a production incident costs hours and user trust. Types measurably reduce defect rates and make onboarding faster because the contracts are self-describing.
foundations.engineeringImpact: Types make large refactors safe and turn the editor into a guide. A change to a component's API surfaces everywhere it is consumed, so you fix all call sites in one pass instead of discovering them through bug reports.
foundations.performanceImpact: There is zero runtime performance cost — types are erased during compilation. The only cost is build/type-check time, which is offset by far less time spent debugging runtime type errors.
commonUseCases: Typing component props with an interface, including optional and required fields
Typing children with React.ReactNode for components that wrap arbitrary content
Annotating useState, useRef, and useReducer with explicit generics
Building generic, reusable components like a typed List<T> or Select<T>
Modeling mutually exclusive props with discriminated unions

commonMisconceptions.myth: React.FC is the recommended way to type every component.
commonMisconceptions.reality: React.FC has fallen out of favor: it historically forced an implicit children prop and complicates generics and defaultProps. Most teams prefer typing the props directly: function Button(props: ButtonProps) { ... }.

commonMisconceptions.myth: useState always infers the right type, so you never need a generic.
commonMisconceptions.reality: It infers from the initial value, but useState(null) infers null and useState([]) infers never[]. When the value can be more than its initial form, supply an explicit type: useState<User | null>(null).

commonMisconceptions.myth: any is a quick, harmless way to satisfy the compiler.
commonMisconceptions.reality: any disables type checking for that value and silently spreads. Prefer unknown (which forces a narrowing check) or a precise type; reserve any for genuine escape hatches.

visualExplorer.title: How a typed component is checked
visualExplorer.caption: Step through how the compiler turns a prop interface into a contract that is verified at every call site, then erased before the browser runs the code.

config.intro: TypeScript checks React code in distinct stages. Walk through what happens from writing a prop type to running plain JavaScript in the browser.

steps.name: Declare the contract
steps.detail: You write an interface (e.g. interface ButtonProps { label: string; onClick: () => void; disabled?: boolean }). This is the component's public API — required and optional fields are explicit.

steps.name: Type the component
steps.detail: The component is a function whose parameter is typed with that interface: function Button({ label, onClick, disabled }: ButtonProps). Inside, every prop now has a known type, so the editor autocompletes and flags misuse.

steps.name: Check call sites
steps.detail: At every <Button .../> usage the compiler verifies the JSX attributes match ButtonProps: a missing label is an error, an extra prop is an error, onClick must be a function. This is where most bugs are caught.

steps.name: Type state, refs, events
steps.detail: Internal values are typed too: useState<number>(0), useRef<HTMLInputElement>(null), and handlers like (e: React.ChangeEvent<HTMLInputElement>) => ... so e.target.value is known to be a string.

steps.name: Compile and erase
steps.detail: tsc (or the bundler's transpiler) checks all types, then strips every annotation and emits plain JavaScript. If any check failed the build can be blocked.

steps.name: Run in the browser
steps.detail: The browser executes the emitted JavaScript with no types present. Runtime behavior is identical to hand-written JS — the entire benefit was the compile-time safety you already collected.

interactiveExamples.title: Typing props with an interface
interactiveExamples.explanation: Props are described with an interface. Optional props use ?. The compiler then enforces that every <Greeting /> supplies a string name and may supply an excited flag.
interactiveExamples.expectedOutput: Two greetings; the first ends with '!' (excited), the second with '.'.

interactiveExamples.title: Typed state and a typed change event
interactiveExamples.explanation: useState<string>('') makes the state a string. The change handler is typed as React.ChangeEvent<HTMLInputElement>, so e.target.value is known to be a string and autocompletes.
interactiveExamples.expectedOutput: An input whose live character count updates as you type.

interactiveExamples.title: A generic, reusable List component
interactiveExamples.explanation: A generic component <T,> works for any item type. The renderItem callback receives an item typed as T, and TypeScript infers T from the items prop — so the callback is fully typed at every call site.
interactiveExamples.expectedOutput: A list of user names, then a list of numbers — both rendered through one generic component.

codeLab.title: Type a Counter component and a useToggle hook
codeLab.instructions: 1) Add a CounterProps interface giving Counter a required `start: number` and optional `step?: number` (default 1). 2) Type the count state as a number. 3) Complete the useToggle custom hook so it returns a typed tuple: [boolean, () => void]. Use the hook in App to show/hide the counter.
codeLab.expectedOutput: A Toggle button that shows/hides a counter starting at 10 and incrementing by the given step.
hints: Give optional props a default in the destructure: ({ step = 1 }: CounterProps).
Annotate the hook's return type explicitly — `: [boolean, () => void]` — so consumers get a typed tuple instead of (boolean | (() => void))[].
useState<number>(start) keeps count a number even though start is passed in.

debuggingLab.title: useState(null) infers the wrong type
debuggingLab.symptom: Accessing user.name reports 'Object is possibly null' or 'Property name does not exist on type never', even though you set a user object later.
debuggingLab.errorAnalysis: useState infers its type from the initial argument. useState(null) infers the literal type null, so the setter only accepts null and reading user.name is invalid. You must tell TypeScript the value can also be a User, and then narrow before reading.
commonMistakes: Calling useState(null) or useState([]) and expecting it to infer the eventual shape.
Reading a possibly-null value without a guard, so the compiler flags 'possibly null'.
debuggingLab.fixChallenge: Give useState an explicit generic of User | null, and guard the render so you only read user.name when user is not null.

theory.question: How do you type a component's props, and why is React.FC often discouraged now?
theory.directAnswer: Define an interface or type for the props and annotate the component's parameter directly: function Button(props: ButtonProps). React.FC is discouraged because it historically added an implicit children prop to every component (even ones that take no children), interacts awkwardly with generics, and complicates default props — typing the props parameter directly is simpler and more explicit.

detailedExplanation.whatItIs: Props typing describes the exact shape of the object a component receives, including which fields are required and which are optional.
detailedExplanation.whyItExists: Without it, JavaScript silently accepts misspelled or missing props. The interface turns the component into a checked function signature.
detailedExplanation.howItWorks: You write `interface ButtonProps { label: string; onClick: () => void; disabled?: boolean }` and destructure in the parameter: function Button({ label, onClick, disabled = false }: ButtonProps). The compiler verifies every <Button /> against that interface.

theory.whyImportant: Props are the public API of a component; typing them is the single highest-value use of TypeScript in React and is asked in nearly every React+TS interview.
theory.realWorldExample: A shared design-system Button exports its ButtonProps interface so consumers get autocomplete and a compile error if they forget the required onClick.

nestedTopics.title: interface vs type
nestedTopics.explanation: Both work for props. interface can be merged/extended and is idiomatic for object shapes; type is needed for unions, intersections, and mapped/conditional types.

nestedTopics.title: Optional props
nestedTopics.explanation: A `?` marks a prop optional (e.g. disabled?: boolean); give it a default in the destructure to avoid scattering undefined checks.

nestedTopics.title: Extending native props
nestedTopics.explanation: Extend React.ComponentPropsWithoutRef<'button'> to inherit all native button attributes (onClick, type, etc.) and add your own.

followUps.question: How do you type children?
followUps.answer: Use React.ReactNode for the children prop — it covers JSX, strings, numbers, arrays, and null, i.e. anything renderable. Define it as `children: React.ReactNode` (or optional with ?).

followUps.question: When would you still use React.FC?
followUps.answer: Rarely — some teams keep it for the explicit return-type and displayName ergonomics, but the modern default is to type props directly and let the return type be inferred.

theory.question: How do you type useState, useRef, and useReducer correctly?
theory.directAnswer: useState infers from its initial value but takes an explicit generic when the eventual type is broader: useState<User | null>(null). useRef takes the element/value type and a null initial for DOM refs: useRef<HTMLInputElement>(null). useReducer is typed by typing its state and action types — usually a State interface and an Action discriminated union — and the reducer signature (state: State, action: Action) => State; the dispatch is then fully typed.

detailedExplanation.whatItIs: Each hook is a generic function whose type argument tells TypeScript what value it manages.
detailedExplanation.whyItExists: Inference works for simple cases but fails for null initials, empty arrays, and union states, so explicit generics restore correctness.
detailedExplanation.howItWorks: useState<T> sets the state and setter types to T. useRef<T>(null) creates a RefObject<T> whose .current is T | null. For useReducer, you type the reducer; TypeScript then infers the state type and constrains dispatch to valid actions.

theory.whyImportant: Mis-typed hooks are the most common React+TS bug source (null states, never[] arrays), so interviewers probe whether you know when inference is enough and when to be explicit.
theory.realWorldExample: A form uses useReducer with an Action discriminated union ({ type: 'setField'; field: string; value: string } | { type: 'reset' }) so the reducer's switch is exhaustively checked.

nestedTopics.title: useState<T | null>
nestedTopics.explanation: For data that starts empty but becomes an object — useState<User | null>(null) — so the setter accepts the object and reads require a null guard.

nestedTopics.title: useRef element vs mutable
nestedTopics.explanation: useRef<HTMLInputElement>(null) for DOM nodes (.current is read-only-ish, possibly null); useRef<number>(0) for a mutable instance variable that doesn't trigger re-renders.

nestedTopics.title: Action discriminated unions
nestedTopics.explanation: Typing actions as a union on a literal `type` field lets the reducer narrow per case and the compiler flag unhandled actions.

followUps.question: Why does useState([]) misbehave?
followUps.answer: It infers never[], so pushing typed items errors. Annotate it: useState<string[]>([]).

followUps.question: Why is a ref's current possibly null?
followUps.answer: DOM refs are null on the first render before the element mounts, so .current is typed T | null and must be guarded.

scenario.question: A Banner component can render either an 'info' variant (requires a `message`) or an 'action' variant (requires a `message` and an `onConfirm` callback). Developers keep passing onConfirm to info banners or forgetting it on action banners. How do you make the type system prevent both mistakes?
scenario.directAnswer: Model the props as a discriminated union keyed on a literal `variant` field: type BannerProps = { variant: 'info'; message: string } | { variant: 'action'; message: string; onConfirm: () => void }. Now the compiler requires onConfirm only when variant is 'action' and rejects it on 'info', and inside the component a switch on variant narrows the props.

detailedExplanation.whatItIs: A discriminated (tagged) union is a union of object types that share a common literal field used to tell them apart.
detailedExplanation.whyItExists: A single flat interface with optional fields can't express 'these props are required together' — optionals let invalid combinations through. A union encodes mutually exclusive shapes.
detailedExplanation.howItWorks: TypeScript narrows the union by the discriminant (variant). In the 'action' branch onConfirm is known to exist; in 'info' it's known not to. JSX usage is checked the same way at the call site.

scenario.whyImportant: Discriminated unions for props is a senior-level pattern interviewers love because it shows you can make invalid states unrepresentable rather than relying on runtime checks.

nestedTopics.title: Discriminant field
nestedTopics.explanation: A common literal property (here `variant`) is what lets TypeScript narrow the union; without it the compiler can't tell the shapes apart.

nestedTopics.title: Exhaustiveness
nestedTopics.explanation: Add a default case asserting `never` so adding a new variant without handling it is a compile error.

followUps.question: Why not just make onConfirm optional?
followUps.answer: Optional allows the invalid combinations (action without onConfirm, info with onConfirm). The whole point of the union is to forbid those at compile time.

coding.question: Write a fully typed custom hook useLocalStorage<T> that syncs a value to localStorage and returns a typed [value, setValue] tuple.
coding.thoughtProcess: I make the hook generic over T so it works for any serializable value. The return type is annotated as [T, (v: T) => void] (or React.Dispatch) so consumers get a typed tuple, not a loose array. State is initialized lazily by reading and JSON-parsing localStorage, and an effect writes back on change. I keep the example runnable with a plain App that uses the hook.
coding.lineByLine: The hook is generic over T. The return type is annotated [T, (value: T) => void] so the tuple stays typed. useState<T> with a lazy initializer reads and parses localStorage once. update sets state and writes the JSON back. In App, useLocalStorage<string> instantiates T as string, so name is a string and the change handler's e.target.value type-checks.
coding.timeComplexity: O(1) per read/write apart from JSON.stringify/parse, which is O(n) in the serialized size.
coding.spaceComplexity: O(n) in the size of the stored value.

alternativeApproaches.title: Return React.Dispatch<React.SetStateAction<T>>
alternativeApproaches.explanation: Expose the full setter type so consumers can pass an updater function (prev => next), matching useState's ergonomics, at the cost of a slightly more complex signature.

followUps.question: Why annotate the return type instead of letting it infer?
followUps.answer: Without the annotation, TypeScript widens the tuple to an array type (T | ((value: T) => void))[], so destructuring loses precise per-position types. The explicit [T, (value: T) => void] preserves the tuple.

productionDeepDive.architecture: Co-locate prop types with the component and export them when the component is shared. Prefer composing types: extend React.ComponentPropsWithoutRef<'button'> to inherit native attributes instead of re-declaring them. Use discriminated unions to make invalid prop combinations unrepresentable rather than validating at runtime.
productionDeepDive.performance: Types are erased at build time, so there is no runtime cost. The trade-off is type-check time on large codebases — keep types reasonably simple, avoid deeply recursive conditional types in hot paths, and enable incremental builds (tsc --incremental / project references) to keep CI fast.
productionDeepDive.security: Treat external data (fetch responses, props from untrusted sources) as unknown and validate/parse it (e.g. with a schema library like Zod) before trusting the type. A type assertion (`as User`) lies to the compiler and offers no runtime guarantee — never assert your way past untrusted input.
productionDeepDive.scaling: As the codebase grows, share types via a central types module or per-feature type files, and turn on strict mode (strict: true) early. Strict null checks in particular prevent a huge class of 'undefined is not an object' production crashes.
productionDeepDive.maintainability: Let return types infer for components and small functions, but annotate public hook and utility return types so a change there can't silently alter every consumer's inferred type. Avoid any; use unknown plus narrowing at boundaries.
productionDeepDive.observability: The type checker itself is your earliest signal — wire `tsc --noEmit` into pre-commit and CI so type regressions fail the build. Editor diagnostics surface most issues before code is even committed.

caseStudies.problem: A widely-used component had an optional prop that was actually required in half its usages, causing runtime crashes when omitted.
caseStudies.solution: Replaced the optional prop with a discriminated union so each variant declared exactly the props it needed.
caseStudies.tradeoffs: Slightly more verbose prop type vs eliminating a whole category of runtime errors.
caseStudies.lessons: Encode 'these props go together' in the type system; optional props that are conditionally required are a common source of bugs.

projectBuilder.summary: Add TypeScript types to the dashboard's components: a typed UsersTable, a generic reusable Table<T>, typed filter state, and a typed useUsers hook.
requirements: A User interface and a typed UsersTable that consumes User[]
A generic Table<T> component with a typed columns/renderCell API
Typed filter state and a typed change handler for the search input
A typed useUsers() hook returning { users, loading, error }
projectBuilder.architecture: Define shared interfaces (User, Column<T>) in a types module. The Table component is generic over its row type; the dashboard instantiates Table<User>. Filter state is typed (e.g. status: 'all' | 'active' | 'inactive'), and the data hook returns a typed object so consumers get autocomplete on users/loading/error.
projectBuilder.folderStructure:
src/
  types/
    user.ts
  components/
    Table.tsx
    UsersTable.tsx
    SearchBar.tsx
  hooks/
    useUsers.ts

steps.title: Define domain types
steps.instructions: Create a User interface and a generic Column<T> type with key and a render function.
steps.checkpoint: Importing User gives autocomplete on its fields.

steps.title: Build a generic Table<T>
steps.instructions: Type Table so it accepts rows: T[] and columns: Column<T>[]; instantiate it as Table<User> in UsersTable.
steps.checkpoint: Passing the wrong row shape is a compile error.

steps.title: Type filter state and handler
steps.instructions: Type the status filter as a union of literals and the search handler as React.ChangeEvent<HTMLInputElement>.
steps.checkpoint: Assigning an invalid status value fails to compile.

steps.title: Type the data hook
steps.instructions: Make useUsers return a typed { users: User[]; loading: boolean; error: string | null }.
steps.checkpoint: Consumers get autocomplete and null-safety on the hook's result.

enhancements: Validate the fetched users with a schema (e.g. Zod) and infer the User type from the schema
Add a discriminated union for the hook's state (loading | success | error)
interviewQuestions: Why make the Table component generic instead of hard-coding User?
How would you guarantee the API response actually matches the User type at runtime?

keyTakeaways: Type props with an interface/type and annotate the component parameter directly; prefer this over React.FC.
useState infers from its initial value — pass an explicit generic (useState<User | null>(null), useState<string[]>([])) when the eventual type is broader.
Type events with React's synthetic event types (React.ChangeEvent<HTMLInputElement>, React.MouseEvent, React.FormEvent) so event fields are known.
Annotate custom hook return types (tuples/objects) so consumers get precise, stable contracts.
Use discriminated unions to make invalid prop combinations impossible, and treat external data as unknown until validated.
All types are erased at compile time — there is zero runtime cost; the benefit is entirely compile-time safety and editor tooling.
